name: Pachacuti
info: Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui was the ninth Sapa Inca of Cusco in the fifteenth-century Andes, remembered for transforming a small chiefdom into the Inca Empire, rebuilding Cusco and, most archaeologists believe, building Machu Picchu as his estate.

facts.born: In Cusco, at the palace of Cusicancha, in 1403 according to the historian José Antonio del Busto Duthurburu; given name Cusi Yupanqui, of the lineage Iñaca Panaka, and according to the Spanish chroniclers the son of the eighth ruler, Inca Viracocha
facts.died: 1471 in the standard chronology, of a terminal illness; some colonial sources hint that he had abdicated before his death
facts.role: Ninth Sapa Inca of Cusco, reigning from 1438 to 1471 in John Howland Rowe's chronology (other scholars give 1400–1448, 1410–1450, 1420–1472 or 1425–1471); founder of the imperial lineage Hatun Ayllu
facts.known: Defending Cusco against the Chankas; transforming the Chiefdom of Cusco into the Inca Empire; rebuilding Cusco and the sun temple Qurikancha; Machu Picchu, believed to have been built as his estate; conquests around Lake Titicaca; forced resettlement of colonists (mitimaes); his link with the cult of the sun god Inti

t: In the Inca accounts recorded by Spanish chroniclers, the young Cusi Yupanqui defended Cusco against the Chankas when the ruler fled, took power and renamed himself Pachacuti.

He and his generals began the conquests that within three generations carried Inca rule from the valley of Cusco across a sizeable part of western South America, while he rebuilt Cusco as an imperial city.
The Incas did not count years, the sources are colonial and partisan, and scholars still disagree whether he was a historical emperor or a mythological figure for the start of Inca expansion.
dyk: The familiar form Pachacútec was introduced by the writer Inca Garcilaso de la Vega in 1609 and is ungrammatical in Quechua. Documents of the 16th century write Pachacuti, reconstructed as pacha kutiy, "the turn of the world".
ev: Cusi Yupanqui, the later Pachacuti, is born in Cusco at the palace of Cusicancha, in the year given by the historian José Antonio del Busto Duthurburu
In del Busto's chronology he rallies the army and defends Cusco against the Chankas after the ruler Inca Viracocha and his co-ruler Urco flee
After a short civil war in which Urco dies he is crowned Sapa Inca of Cusco and takes the name Pachacuti, in the same chronology
He names his son Amaru Yupanqui co-ruler, at about the date del Busto gives, and later replaces him with another son, Tupac Yupanqui
Tupac Yupanqui leads his first military campaign around this year according to del Busto; John Howland Rowe has him take military command in 1463
Pachacuti dies of a terminal illness in the standard chronology, and Tupac Inca Yupanqui succeeds him without recorded dispute

sections.early:
Pachacuti's given name was Cusi Yupanqui, or Ripac. He was born in Cusco, at the palace of Cusicancha beside the Inticancha temple, into the lineage of Iñaca Panaka in the moiety of Hanan Cusco, "high Cusco". According to the Spanish chroniclers he was the son of the eighth ruler of Cusco, Inca Viracocha, and he is traditionally considered the son of Viracocha and Mama Runtu. The historian María Rostworowski concluded from the colonial writings that he was not Viracocha's son: Andean custom let the "most able" take power, which the Spaniards, who thought in terms of primogeniture, read as illegitimacy. Catherine Julien holds that Inca legitimacy rested on a concentration of "capac" status, inherited from Manco Capac through both the female and the male line.

The Incas of Cusco did not systematically count years, so every date in his life is an approximation from colonial documents or archaeology. The historian José Antonio del Busto Duthurburu placed his birth in 1403. His tutor, Micuymana, is said to have taught him history, laws and language and the handling of quipus, the knotted cords used for records. In the traditions the chroniclers collected, Inca nobles admired him from a young age for the courage, intelligence and maturity that his brother Inca Urco, the appointed co-ruler and heir, lacked, and Viracocha's generals began to conspire to replace Urco. The main sources for his life are Juan de Betanzos and Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, both drawing on the "life history" kept by his descent group.
sections.rise:
In the early 15th century the Chankas, described as the Incas' traditional enemies, invaded the Cusco confederation. Several versions of the encounter exist; in the one most accepted, the ruler Inca Viracocha and his co-ruler Urco fled, while Cusi Yupanqui rallied the army with four of Viracocha's generals and prepared the city's defence. The Chankas were repelled so severely that, legend tells, even the stones rose up to fight on his side, and at the battle of Yahuar Pampa the Inca army won a decisive victory. Cusi Yupanqui brought captured Chanka leaders to his father to tread upon, a traditional victory ritual. Viracocha answered that the honour belonged to the designated heir, Urco. A heated argument followed, and Viracocha tried to have him assassinated; the plot failed.

Viracocha went into exile, and Inca Yupanqui returned in triumph to Cusco. After a short civil war in which Urco died he was crowned Sapa Inca and took the name Pachacuti, from a Quechua concept meaning "the turn of the world", a cataclysmic change of eras. The ethnic groups around Cusco that had helped him received the status of "hawa inka", Incas by privilege. An exact date for the war is not known. Del Busto put the defence of Cusco in 1424 and the reign from 1425; John Howland Rowe's standard chronology of 1945 begins the reign in 1438, though radiocarbon dates suggest the beginning of the 15th century. Since the early 1980s the academic consensus, following Pierre Duviols, has treated the Chanka attack as largely mythical; Terence N. D'Altroy allows that the saga may contain historical elements.
sections.deeds:
Despite his prestige Pachacuti at first had "little effective power and a meager work force". He summoned the surrounding chiefs, the kurakas, to Cusco for lavish feasts and gifts, including the booty of the Chanka war, and then made growing demands under the Andean principle of reciprocity: warehouses, stocks of produce, an army, better roads. By these means he rebuilt much of Cusco as an imperial city, with a sector for each of the four suyus, and rebuilt the great sun temple Qurikancha. He is often linked to the origin and spread of the cult of the sun god Inti, and according to Garcilaso de la Vega he created the festival of Inti Raymi. He conquered lands along the Urubamba valley, where most archaeologists believe Machu Picchu was built as his estate. He built irrigation networks, terraces, roads and hospices.

His first campaign, led in person with his general Apo Mayta, struck the Chankas' former allies and the chiefdoms around Cusco. He then defeated the Colla chiefdom of Lake Titicaca at Ayaviri, capturing its ruler, occupied Hatunqulla and received the submission of the Lupacas, Pacasas and Azangaros. Afterwards he left command to his generals. Capac Yupanqui won the submission of Chincha on the coast and marched north as far as Cajamarca; Pachacuti's son Topa Inca Yupanqui forced the Chimú ruler Minchançaman to surrender by cutting the irrigation canals that fed his capital, Chan Chan, and campaigned in what is now Ecuador. Scholars differ on how much of this was lasting conquest: Rowe judged the Chincha and Cajamarca campaigns to have been raids.
sections.opponents:
Pachacuti's rule began in conflict with his own house: his father Viracocha tried to have him killed and his brother Urco died in the civil war that brought him to power. He spent the first months of his reign putting down revolts by chiefs of the Cusco valley. While an expedition was in the eastern lowlands, the Colla, Lupaca and Azangaro rose under a son of the former Colla ruler; according to Sarmiento de Gamboa an army of around 200,000 men was assembled to put the revolt down. The accounts also record that he had two of his brothers, the general Capac Yupanqui and Huayna Yupanqui, killed after the northern campaign, and that he killed his sons Tilca Yupanqui and Auqui Yupanqui.

He began the practice of forced migration, sending colonists called mitimaes from loyal areas to unstable provinces, and is credited with displacing hundreds of thousands of people to the remote edges of the empire; these colonists held the lowest place in the Inca social order. The record itself is contested. Sarmiento's history, commissioned by the Viceroy of Peru, was written partly to justify Spanish rule, and Betanzos altered the story to place his wife's ancestor in the succession. Various historians associate Pachacuti with rewriting the reigns of earlier rulers to justify expansion. Pierre Duviols, Reiner Tom Zuidema, Juan Ossio Acuña, Gary Urton and Franck Garcia regard him as mythological or mytho-historical; Zuidema wrote that the rulers before Topa Inca Yupanqui were social groups or factions. Rowe, Rostworowski, Julien, Martti Pärssinen and others consider him historical.
sections.last:
Having conquered the nations around Cusco in person, Pachacuti withdrew from campaigning to concentrate on administrative reforms and the embellishment of the city. Following Inca custom he named his crown prince, Amaru Yupanqui, co-ruler, to test his capacities and to avoid a war of succession. The traditions describe Amaru as a gentle man given to agriculture and the building of canals, "too human to be ruler". After 5 to 6 or 10 years, finding him without military talent, Pachacuti presented another son, Tupac Yupanqui, to the Inca nobles, who elected him co-ruler; other sources say Amaru's reign ended on his mother's death, because the nobility disdained him. Rostworowski suggested a reign of around 60 years in all: 40 alone, 5 to 6 with Amaru and 14 to 15 with Tupac Yupanqui.

In his last years government may in practice have lain with a "helper" or "brother" named Yamqui Yupanqui, who at Pachacuti's death confirmed Tupac Inca Yupanqui as successor. Pachacuti died in 1471, in the standard chronology, of a terminal illness, and his son succeeded without any recorded dispute. Some colonial sources hint that he had abdicated before his death. Some historians place a brief independent reign of Amaru Yupanqui after his death, ended by Tupac Yupanqui. Sarmiento de Gamboa attributed a song to him on his deathbed: "I was born as a lily in the garden, and like the lily I grew, as my age advanced / I became old and had to die, and so I withered and died." His mummy was taken at his own wish to the palace of Patallacta and was later found at Tococache.
sections.legacy:
Pachacuti began an era of conquest that within three generations expanded Inca rule from the valley of Cusco to a sizeable part of western South America. He did not improve the system of succession: in later generations each new Inca had to win enough support from the nobles, the priesthood and the army to prevail in a civil war or deter rivals. His deeds were handed down in genealogical histories, life histories and quipus kept near his royal mummy by his lineage, Hatun Ayllu; his life history began with the Chanka attack and ended with his death and the short poem attributed to him. He is also remembered as a poet, the author of the Sacred Hymns of the Situa.

In Andean cosmology he stands beside the creator deity Viracocha and the mythical first Inca, Manco Cápac, as the archetype of the perfect Inca ruler, who spread the Inca cultural model and pantheon among the peoples of the Andes. Modern scholarship is divided over what lies behind that figure. Rowe, comparing the colonial sources, argued for a state-sanctioned "standard history" in which the victory over the Chankas caused the imperial expansion, and Rostworowski's biography of 1953 supported him. Zuidema and Duviols concluded that the Inca state was a diarchy in which Pachacuti had a co-ruler, and Pärssinen that Cusco had three rulers. Catherine Julien found in 2009 that Zuidema's structuralism reorients the search for a meaningful Inca history but takes no account of change. Pachacuti appears today as the leader of the Incas in video games, novels and television series.

summary: Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui, ninth ruler of Cusco in the 15th century, is credited with defeating the Chankas, rebuilding Cusco and beginning the conquests that made the Inca Empire. His story reaches us through colonial chroniclers, and scholars disagree on its dates and on how far it is history or myth. Machu Picchu is thought to have been his estate.
references: María Rostworowski, Pachacútec Inca Yupanqui (Instituto de Estudios Peruanos, 2001)
María Rostworowski, History of the Inca Realm (Cambridge University Press, 1999)
Catherine Julien, Reading Inca History (University of Iowa Press, 2000)
Pedro Sarmiento De Gamboa, History Of The Incas (CreateSpace Independent Publishing Platform, 2011)
notes: DATES: the article gives no birth date of its own. start 1403 is del Busto's figure only (circa true). end 1471 is stated flatly in 'Death and succession' and is Rowe's/del Busto's end of reign; other chronologies in the article end the reign in 1448, 1450 or 1472, and Baptista Gumucio and García Ortiz put his death before 1478. endCirca set true.

EVENTS: because the Incas did not count years, the six events rest on del Busto's chronology (1403, 1424, 1425, c. 1450, c. 1461) and the 1471 death; each sentence says whose date it is. The article has 'around 1461' and 'around 1450' but gives 1403, 1424 and 1425 without 'around'; I marked all 'c.' given the article's own statement that all dates are approximations. Editor may prefer fewer events - but five is the minimum.
'Sarmiento de Gamboa an army of around 200.000 men': written 200,000.
The article gives the meaning of the name Pachacuti both as 'the turn of the world' and, in the Rise section, as 'Earth Shaker'; I used the former.

The article contradicts itself on the religious change: the cult of Viracocha 'possibly replaced by the Inti Sun cult' versus sources that have him institute Viracocha as principal deity, and the Coricancha rebuilt 'in honor of Viracocha'. I wrote only that he 'is often linked to the origin and spread of the cult of Inti' (lead).
'in what is now Ecuador': the article says 'regional chiefdoms of modern-day Ecuador' and that Pärssinen thinks territories north of Tomebamba and Cañar were perhaps conquered after his reign.
The wife's name is spelt Mama Anawarkhi / Anarwakhi / Coya Anahuarque in the article; I left her out for length (her marriage is in the Reign section).
'the knotted cords used for records' is my gloss of quipus: the article says only that quipus held information 'according to colour, order and number'. Cut if the editor wants article-only wording.
'described as the Incas' traditional enemies': the article says 'traditional tribal archenemies'.
'the nobles' in the legacy section renders the article's 'apos'.

Capac Yupanqui: the article calls him a general, and in Lineage a brother Pachacuti had killed; 'some ethno-historians however think that Capac Yupanqui was the co-ruler or Huauque (lit. brother)'. I wrote 'two of his brothers, the general Capac Yupanqui and Huayna Yupanqui'.
The article says both 'He was the first Inca ruler to abdicate' (Lineage) and that only 'some colonial sources hint at' an abdication; I kept the hedge.
The Legacy section of the article holds only popular culture; the legacy text is built from the lead, Historicity, Reforms and Death sections.

Left out for length (all in the article): the pre-coronation name Inga Yupangui, the painted wooden panels recording earlier rulers, Murúa as the source for the abdication, Rowe's 1463 for Tupac Yupanqui's command (it is in the c. 1461 event).
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
